# The this Pointer and Constant Member Functions

::: notes
Slides 5-20
:::

<!-- Slide 5 -->

---

## The Problem

You have an object named <code>myWidget</code>. You need to make a copy of it named <code>yourWidget</code>. How can one object refer to its own state while a member function is running?

<!-- Slide 6 -->

---

## Problem

A class has a data member and a member-function parameter with the same name. The function must distinguish the object's member from the local parameter.

<!-- Slide 7 -->

---

## <span style="display:none">No title</span>

<div style="font-size:50%">

~~~cpp
// 11-1x.cpp -- this demo problem
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class Example {
private:
    int x;

public:
    Example(int a) { x = a; }
    void setValue(int);
    void printAddressAndValue();
};

void Example::setValue(int a) {
    x = a;
}

void Example::printAddressAndValue() {
    int x = 50;
    cout << "Object at address: " << " ??? "
         << " has x value: " << x << endl;
}

int main() {
    Example obj1(10);
    Example obj2(20);

    obj1.printAddressAndValue();
    obj2.printAddressAndValue();

    return 0;
}

// How do we print out the class variable x?
~~~

</div>

::: notes
Source file: cpp/11-1x.cpp
The problem asks how to print the class variable x instead of the local variable.
:::

<!-- Slide 8 -->

---

## Object References

A member function operates on the object that receives the call. Inside that function, the current object can be referred to through the implicit <code>this</code> pointer.

<!-- Slide 9 -->

---

## this Pointer

- <code>this</code> points to the object whose member function is running.
- It is available inside non-static member functions.
- <code>this->member</code> selects a data member belonging to the current object.

<!-- Slide 10 -->

---

## Object State and this

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
<div style="font-size:50%">

~~~cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class Example {
private:
    int x;

public:
    Example(int value) { x = value; }
    void printAddressAndValue();
};

void Example::printAddressAndValue() {
    int x = 50;
    cout << "Object address: " << this
         << " has x value: " << this->x << endl;
}

int main() {
    Example obj1(10);
    Example obj2(20);

    obj1.printAddressAndValue();
    obj2.printAddressAndValue();

    return 0;
}
~~~

</div>
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
**Answer**

<code>this</code> points to the object whose member function is running.

<code>this-&gt;x</code> selects the object's data member, so the two calls report values <code>10</code> and <code>20</code>. The local <code>x</code> remains <code>50</code>.
:::
:::

<!-- Slide 11 -->

---

## Code Example: this and Object State

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
<div style="font-size:50%">

~~~cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class Example {
private:
    int x;

public:
    void setValue(int x) {
        this->x = x;
    }

    int getValue() const {
        return this->x;
    }
};

int main() {
    Example item;
    item.setValue(42);
    cout << item.getValue() << endl;

    return 0;
}
~~~

</div>
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
**Output**

~~~text
42
~~~

The parameter <code>x</code> and the data member <code>x</code> have the same name. <code>this->x</code> identifies the member that belongs to the current object.
:::
:::

<!-- Slide 12 -->

---

## Constructors Destructors and this Pointer

- Constructors establish an object's initial state.
- Destructors release resources when an object leaves its lifetime.
- The <code>this</code> pointer identifies the current object inside its member functions.

<!-- Slide 13 -->

---

## What’s Going On?

A member function receives an implicit pointer to the object that called it. The expression <code>this->member</code> makes that relationship visible.

<!-- Slide 14 -->

---

## Use Case

We want to create a <code>Rec</code> class and add two rectangle-like objects together. First, we will use an ordinary function. Then we will move the operation into the class.

<!-- Slide 15 -->

---

## First Example

Let’s build an <code>Add()</code> function that receives two <code>Rec</code> objects and returns a third object containing their combined values.

<!-- Slide 16 -->

---

## Add Function

~~~cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class Rec {
    int x;
    int y;

public:
    Rec(int xx = 1, int yy = 1) {
        x = xx;
        y = yy;
    }

    void print() const {
        cout << x << " by " << y << endl;
    }

    int getX() const { return x; }
    int getY() const { return y; }
};

Rec Add(const Rec& lhs, const Rec& rhs) {
    return Rec(lhs.getX() + rhs.getX(),
               lhs.getY() + rhs.getY());
}

int main() {
    Rec a(5, 5);
    Rec b(5, 5);
    Rec c = Add(a, b);

    c.print();
    return 0;
}
~~~

The free function needs public accessors because it is not a member of <code>Rec</code>.

<!-- Slide 17 -->

---

## Second Example

Let’s make <code>Add()</code> a method instead. The left-hand object becomes the current object, represented by <code>this</code>.

<!-- Slide 18 -->

---

## Add Method

~~~cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class Rec {
    int x;
    int y;

public:
    Rec(int xx = 1, int yy = 1) {
        x = xx;
        y = yy;
    }

    void print() const {
        cout << x << " by " << y << endl;
    }

    Rec add(const Rec& rhs) const {
        Rec result(this->x + rhs.x,
                   this->y + rhs.y);
        return result;
    }
};

int main() {
    Rec a(5, 5);
    Rec b(5, 5);
    Rec c = a.add(b);

    c.print();
    return 0;
}
~~~

As a member function, <code>add</code> can access private data directly.

<!-- Slide 19 -->

---

## What this Means

- Adding primitive operations to objects makes the objects more useful.
- A member function can manipulate private data without a separate getter for every field.
- Constructors can create the result object inside a member operation.

<!-- Slide 20 -->
